category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: RFLA: A Stealthy Reflected Light Adversarial Attack in the Physical World
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
key_idea: A mirror, coloured transparent plastic sheets and a paper cut-out throw sunlight or flashlight shapes onto a target; shape, colour and position are optimised by particle swarm search to flip classifier output.
method: Circle-based parametrisation of reflected-light polygons; particle swarm optimisation of position, geometry, colour and transparency; seven colour sheets measured to correct the colour shift of reflected light.
data: ImageNet-compatible set (1000 images), GTSRB, LISA; ImageNet classifiers plus GTSRB-CNN and LISA-CNN sign classifiers; physical test with six printed images photographed from 2 m (48 photos per light source).
reported_result: Over 99% digital success rate (abstract); physical success rate above 80% for three classifiers (81.25% with sunlight, 87.5% with a flashlight); authors state it is hard to stay effective in fog and rain.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: the reflected-light attack named on the slide. Supplies visible coloured reflection shapes on signs for the controlled attack videos; no detector is proposed (authors only suggest multimodal systems).
code_or_data: https://github.com/winterwindwang/RFLA (seen in search result, not opened) UNVERIFIED
notes: Crossref record and arXiv 2307.07653 both match. Body-text extracts (method, evaluation, conclusion) read through a search result. Physical tests used static printed images, not moving video; camera model not read.

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: Adversarial Laser Beam: Effective Physical-World Attack to DNNs in a Blink
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
key_idea: Visible laser beams with chosen wavelength, angle, width and intensity are added to an image or shone at a real object; a greedy black-box search finds beam settings that cause misclassification.
method: Physical beam parameters (wavelength 380-750 nm, line layout, width, intensity) searched greedily with random restarts using only confidence scores; beam added to the image by linear fusion.
data: 1000 ImageNet images (ResNet50); indoor test with a banana, a conch and a stop sign under three 5 mW laser pointers (450, 532, 680 nm) photographed with a phone; outdoor stop sign test.
reported_result: 95.1% digital success with 834 queries on average; 100% indoor; 77.43% in the outdoor stop-sign test; training with random laser-beam augmentation lowered success to 77.2% on ResNet50. Authors state dynamic environments are not covered.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: laser-beam baseline. Visible beams leave thin saturated streaks, a distinct image cue; tests are static, so view- and time-dependent behaviour is untested.
code_or_data: https://github.com/RjDuan/Advlight (seen in search result, not opened) UNVERIFIED
notes: Crossref and arXiv records both match. Body-text extracts read through a search result.

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: Adversarial catoptric light: An effective, stealthy and robust physical-world attack to DNNs
key_idea: Reflected-light (catoptric) patches with chosen position, colour and intensity are projected onto a target using coloured lamps; a genetic algorithm tunes triangle patches that resemble natural glare on a sign.
method: Genetic-algorithm search over catoptric-light polygon, colour and intensity; expectation over transformation for digital-to-physical transfer; physical test with coloured lamps and an iPhone 6s camera.
data: 1000 ImageNet images (ResNet50) digitally; physical indoor test with 30 samples; outdoor street-sign test with 103 samples; stop sign from several angles.
reported_result: 83.5% success in the outdoor street-sign test and 100% indoors; above 80% success on several DNNs. Authors list a weaker effect in daylight and no attack on non-planar objects.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: mirror-style reflection that looks like benign glare on a sign, the hard-negative pair for a reflection residual. Physical test used lamps, not sunlight on moving video.
notes: Crossref record (IET Computer Vision 2024) matches; arXiv 2209.11739 is dated 2022 and capitalises the title differently. The 83.5% outdoor figure appears in both. Body extracts read in the arXiv HTML through a search result.

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: Adversarial Laser Spot: Robust and Covert Physical-World Attack to DNNs
venue: Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML), PMLR 189
key_idea: Small laser spots (green in the physical tests), tuned by a genetic algorithm in position and colour, fool classifiers; authors claim this is the first light-based physical attack that works in daytime.
method: Genetic algorithm over spot centre and colour; digital samples first, then the physical parameters are replayed with a laser pointer.
data: ImageNet-style classifiers digitally; indoor physical test; outdoor stop sign photographed at 0, 30 and 45 degrees.
reported_result: Outdoor stop-sign success 80.56% at 0 degrees, 77.78% at 30 and 41.67% at 45 degrees; 100% indoors. Authors report better query efficiency than AdvLB but lower digital success.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: daytime laser-spot attack on signs; the drop at 45 degrees shows view dependence that a view-conditioned cue has to model.

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: SLAP: Improving Physical Adversarial Examples with Short-Lived Adversarial Perturbations
key_idea: A light projector casts a crafted perturbation onto a stop sign so the adversarial example can be switched on and off; the projection avoids the patch cues that the SentiNet detector looks for.
method: Projector-based perturbation optimised for robustness to angle, distance and ambient light; tested against object detectors, sign classifiers, SentiNet and adversarial-learning defences.
data: Stop signs; Mask R-CNN, YOLOv3, LISA-CNN and GTSRB-CNN; indoor and outdoor ambient light; approach video from 18 m to about 7 m.
reported_result: Up to 99% success on state-of-the-art networks in non-bright settings; bypasses SentiNet; an adaptive adversarial-learning defender thwarts up to 80% of the attack effect even for a favourable attacker (abstract wording).
relation_to_project: Slides 03 and 04: projected-light attack that already evades a patch detector, so patch-oriented baselines may not transfer to light attacks.
notes: arXiv API record matches (dated 2020). Acceptance at USENIX Security 2021 is stated in the arXiv listing text; the USENIX page was not opened. Check the published version before citing.

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: LaserGuider: A Laser Based Physical Backdoor Attack against Deep Neural Networks
key_idea: Laser spots act as triggers of a physical backdoor in traffic-sign classifiers: poisoned models misread signs only while a laser spot is projected. The authors also release LaserMark, real sign photos with laser spots.
method: Poisoning with digitally simulated laser triggers; laser parameter optimisation; physical test on real laser-stamped signs.
data: LaserMark: 676 sign photos with red, green or blue laser spots (235, 224, 217) plus 158 clean photos, 32 sign classes, iPhone 12 mini, 5-30 m, urban streets.
reported_result: 90.5%, 93.2% and 95.3% attack success for the red, green and blue triggers with negligible impact on clean inputs (paper wording).
relation_to_project: Slide 03: only dataset seen with real laser spots on real signs; possible attack-side test images if the licence allows. Backdoor setting differs from a frozen-detector setting.

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: Invisible Reflections: Leveraging Infrared Laser Reflections to Target Traffic Sign Perception
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS)
key_idea: An infrared laser spot on a sign is invisible to people but appears as false-colour speckle in cameras without an infrared filter, causing misclassification; a speckle colour and frequency detector is proposed.
method: Image-difference modelling of laser traces, frame interpolation of traces, black-box optimisation of spot position, diameter and power; detector masks speckle colours, then thresholds high spatial frequency (over 1% of the region).
data: Four IR-sensitive cameras; single-stage and two-stage sign recognition models (ARTS, GTSRB, LISA, COCO-trained); indoor static and outdoor moving-vehicle tests (5, 8, 13 km/h from 12 m); detector test with 75 benign and 75 attack images per time of day.
reported_result: Up to 100% attack success indoors and at least 80.5% outdoors with a moving vehicle; PatchCleanser mis-certifies at least 33.5% of cases; detector 96% true positives with 2.7% false positives by day and 92% with 6.7% at night (preliminary, 150 images per condition).
relation_to_project: Slide 03: the NDSS 2024 IR-reflection attack with detection named on the slide, and the closest published detector for a reflection-type attack. Its cue is single-frame colour plus spatial frequency, with no view or illumination conditioning and no abstain state. Applies only to cameras without an IR-cut filter.
notes: Crossref DOI matches; the arXiv text prints another DOI (ndss.2024.231053) that Crossref does not hold. Detector numbers and camera details come from body-text extracts of the arXiv HTML read through a search result. Authors say an IR-cut filter would stop the attack but also removes the benefit of IR light for night obstacle detection.

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: WIP: Infrared Laser Reflection Attack Against Traffic Sign Recognition Systems
venue: Symposium on Vehicle Security and Privacy (VehicleSec)
key_idea: Early version of the infrared laser reflection attack: an invisible laser spot on a sign alters filterless-camera images; the paper says patch defences might apply, but their effect on infrared traces is unknown.
method: Image-difference trace modelling; Tree-structured Parzen Estimator search of the beam position; indoor test with a 51.4 mW laser at 3 m, 15 cm spot, 100 lux.
data: GTSRB and LISA CNN classifiers; real stop and 25 mph signs indoors; four backgrounds; 10 frames per case.
reported_result: 100% success on stop and speed-limit signs indoors versus 6.75% (stop) and 34% (speed limit) for a random-position baseline; simulation consistency at least 80%.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: precursor of the NDSS 2024 paper. States that empirical patch defences fall to adaptive attacks and certified ones are costly, and that their effect on infrared traces is unknown.
notes: Crossref record matches. Work-in-progress paper; body extracts read through a search result.

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: I Can See the Light: Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles Using Invisible Lights
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
key_idea: Infrared light invisible to people triggers vehicle camera sensors and appears magenta in the image; it can fake traffic lights and objects and inject SLAM errors. A software detection module is proposed.
method: Off-the-shelf infrared sources aimed at the camera; analysis of the magenta response; software detection built on features of infrared light.
data: Tesla Model 3 and an enterprise-level autonomous driving platform in various environments (abstract).
reported_result: Abstract gives no numbers; authors state the attack works on the two platforms and that vendors had not considered it.
relation_to_project: Slide 03 limitation line: infrared appears as a magenta response on a production-vehicle camera, which gives a spectral cue and fixes the sensor assumption (camera without IR-cut filter).
notes: Crossref record matches; abstract read on the ACM page through a search result.

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: The Spectrum Strikes Back: Infrared POV Attacks on Traffic Sign Classification
key_idea: A rotating near-infrared LED persistence-of-vision display shows remotely switchable patterns on a sign, invisible to people and blocked by a near-infrared cut-off filter; a saturation-based software detector is proposed.
method: Optimal display position found in digital simulation; physical tests with a Sony IMX708 module without infrared filter; detector finds saturated regions and checks for red and blue values above green nearby (sensor-specific).
data: Two signs (stop, 30 km/h), 12 models, distances up to 20 m, varying illumination; detector evaluated on more than 180k images.
reported_result: High attack success across scenarios; with a cut-off filter all images were classified correctly (mean confidence about 93%); detector true-negative rate 99.97-100% and true-positive rate 55.45-98.89% depending on the test case.
relation_to_project: Slide 03: newest infrared attack in this catalog, with hardware (filter) and software defences. Its saturation plus colour-channel anomaly is a cheap local cue close to the slide specular and saturation ROI, but sensor-specific; the filter defence conflicts with low-light perception.
notes: arXiv API record matches; preprint dated 2026, not peer reviewed per the record read. Detector and filter numbers come from body extracts of the arXiv HTML read through a search result.

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: Targeted Physical Evasion Attacks in the Near-Infrared Domain
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS)
key_idea: An off-the-shelf infrared flashlight shines a transparent-film pattern onto a sign, giving targeted and untargeted infrared perturbations without lasers; a Segment-Anything shape-count detector flags the added edges.
method: Film-projected infrared transformation optimised digitally and replayed physically; detector counts Segment Anything (ViT-L) masks and thresholds the count.
data: Traffic signs in digital and physical tests, static and from a moving vehicle; detection data 54 benign and 400 adversarial static images plus 476 benign and 1158 adversarial moving-vehicle images.
reported_result: Targeted success up to 99.4% in moving-vehicle tests; authors say the attack costs under 50 USD; test-time defences and adversarial training only reduce success to about 62-68%; shape-count detector F1 up to 99% static and 85% moving.
relation_to_project: Slides 03 and 05: authors argue frame-consistency defences have limited effect when the attack is consistent over most frames (163-frame clip, 0.6% flicker) and that speckle detection needs coherent light. A brightness-agnostic shape count is a cheap explainable cue, but it uses a large model whose latency is not given in the extracts read.
code_or_data: https://rub-infsec.github.io/infrared_perturbations/ (project page seen in a search result) UNVERIFIED

category: A3-F2 Infrared and invisible-light attacks and their detection
title: Invisible Optical Adversarial Stripes on Traffic Sign against Autonomous Vehicles
venue: ACM International Conference on Mobile Systems, Applications and Services (MobiSys)
key_idea: Modulated LED light exploits the camera rolling shutter to paint stripes on a sign that people cannot see; the emission timing adapts to camera operation and vehicle motion so recognition stays wrong across frames.
method: GhostStripe controls the timing of modulated light emission relative to the rolling-shutter readout; countermeasures are discussed at sensor, model and system level.
data: Real testbeds with a moving victim vehicle.
reported_result: Spoofs the recognition result to a wrong class for up to 94% of frames while the vehicle passes the road section (abstract).
relation_to_project: Slides 03 and 04: light attack invisible to people but fully visible to an IR-filtered camera, so it sits outside the IR limit of slide 03; persistent across frames, which matters for slide 05.
notes: arXiv API record matches and carries a MobiSys 2024 journal reference (pages 534-546); venue page not opened. Closest to slide 04.

venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
key_idea: Fluorescent ink on a sign is triggered by invisible ultraviolet light, producing a perturbation that misleads traffic sign recognition; the attack is modelled digitally to pick optimal fluorescence settings.

title: Detecting and Identifying Optical Signal Attacks on Autonomous Driving Systems
key_idea: With three sensors the framework builds two disparity maps and flags optical attacks from the distribution of disparity errors; an identification model then finds which sensor is attacked.
method: Two depth versions from three sensors; distribution analysis of disparity errors; identification scheme with a correctness proof for up to n-2 attacked sensors (one LiDAR, n cameras).

category: A3-F3 Retroreflective-material attacks at night
title: WIP: Adversarial Retroreflective Patches: A Novel Stealthy Attack on Traffic Sign Recognition at Night
venue: Symposium on Vehicle Security and Privacy (VehicleSec)
key_idea: Retroreflective patches matching the sign colour are inconspicuous by day and return headlight light to the camera at night, disturbing sign recognition; preliminary feasibility study with digital and physical tests.
method: Digital simulation of the reflection by image processing, then physical patches on a real sign photographed under headlights; YOLOv3-tiny as target.
data: YOLOv3-tiny; real sign with a reflective patch photographed under headlight at 3, 5 and 7 m and at -30, 0 and 30 degrees.
reported_result: 100% success in digital simulation and at most 90% in physical tests (90% at 5 m and 0 degrees, 50% at 3 m and 7 m, 65% at 30 degrees and 35% at -30 degrees); the benign detector missed 0%, 15% and 45% of frames at 3, 5 and 7 m.
relation_to_project: Slide 03 at night: early retroreflective patch attack on signs. Retroreflection is also the normal behaviour of signs under headlights, so a residual has to separate patch-like excess return from normal sheeting. Small evaluation.
notes: Crossref record matches. Work-in-progress paper; numbers come from body extracts read through a search result. An NDSS 2024 poster with the same title and topic exists.

category: A3-F3 Retroreflective-material attacks at night
title: Trapped by Their Own Light: Deployable and Stealth Retroreflective Patch Attacks on Traffic Sign Recognition Systems
key_idea: Retroreflective patches in the sign colour stay hidden by day and return headlight light at night, misleading recognition; a polarizing-filter defence (DPR Shield) on headlight and camera suppresses the patch return.
method: Physics-based retroreflection simulation in Blender (roughness, IoR level, specular tint fitted to measurements), black-box patch optimisation, physical tests with a FLIR Blackfly S camera; defence uses a polarised headlight with a crossed camera filter.
data: ARTS, GTSRB, LISA and Mapillary-trained YOLOv5, Faster R-CNN and CNN models; dusk lux sweeps; driving tests at 5-25 km/h from 15-50 m; two production sign-recognition systems (2024 Toyota Yaris and Nissan e-note); user study with 50 participants.
reported_result: At least 93.4% success in dynamic scenarios at 35 m or more; 60% and 75% success on the two production systems (20 trials each); STOP-sign attack effective only below about 900 lux; DPR Shield cut STOP-sign success from 100% to 0% with benign accuracy at 100% (speed-limit sign two-stage model kept 25%).
relation_to_project: Slide 03 at night: retroreflection is also the benign behaviour of signs under headlights. The paper gives a physics model with entrance and viewing angles and measured lux dependence that a view-conditioned residual can reuse. States that temporal memory in commercial systems lowers success.
notes: arXiv API record matches (arXiv metadata shows a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence). A Waseda lab page seen in a search result states acceptance at ACSAC 2026; not verified on the venue page. Body extracts read through a search result.

category: A3-F3 Retroreflective-material attacks at night
title: Reflective Adversarial Attacks against Pedestrian Detection Systems for Vehicles at Night
key_idea: Reflective microprism patches matching clothing colour are placed by particle swarm search; at night, headlight return disrupts vehicle pedestrian detectors; a symmetry strategy uses a surrogate model for black-box transfer.
method: Particle swarm patch placement on YOLOv5-generated examples; deployment on clothing with 3M DG3 reflective sheeting; night tests with vehicles passing at several distances.
data: Self-made test dataset and KITTI; RetinaNet and other pedestrian detectors; physical night tests.
reported_result: RetinaNet success above 80% on the authors test set and 93.6% on KITTI; after targeted adversarial training success mostly fell but stayed above 20% (RetinaNet 67%).
relation_to_project: Slide 03 at night: retroreflective attack on a pedestrian detector, not signs; shows the headlight-return mechanism reaches object detection, which the slide targets.

category: A3-F3 Retroreflective-material attacks at night
title: Physics-Based Adversarial Attack on Near-Infrared Human Detector for Nighttime Surveillance Camera Systems
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
key_idea: Night-mode surveillance cameras with the IR-cut filter off see near-infrared images where clothing loses colour and texture; retro-reflective and insulating tapes form patterns that hide a person from a YOLO detector.
method: Binary tape patterns designed digitally by black-box query and search, then realised with retro-reflective and electrical-insulation tapes on clothes.
data: Physical tests at 3, 4 and 5 m against a YOLO human detector with a near-infrared surveillance-style camera.
reported_result: Average attack success 87.93% in physical tests (76.22% at 3 m, 91.20% at 4 m, 96.36% at 5 m); average detector confidence 0.088 (arXiv text).

category: A3-F1 Reflected-light and laser attacks
title: Rolling Colors: Adversarial Laser Exploits against Traffic Light Recognition
key_idea: Modulated laser pulses exploit the rolling shutter to inject a colour stripe over a traffic light; the paper catalogues laser effects on images: overexposure, colour shift, stripes, white-balance shift and defocus.
method: Optimisation of laser parameters from empirical interference models; emulated and real set-ups; countermeasure proposed: randomised rolling-shutter row order.
data: Two recognition systems and five cameras; real-world tests including a moving vehicle at over 40 m.
reported_result: Maximum success 30% (red to green) and 86.25% (green to red); effective over consecutive frames from over 40 m against a moving vehicle (abstract).
relation_to_project: Slides 03 and 04: laser effects on the sensor itself (saturation, single-channel colour shift, white-balance shift) are artefact signatures a cheap local residual can measure. Traffic lights, not signs; the countermeasure is a sensor redesign, not a detector.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed per the record read. Artefact list read from body extracts of the arXiv page through a search result.
